deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler's 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina', Chapter 3, on the sum-of-divisors function, which he writes ∫N and we write σ(N) (all divisors, N included). The previous page established multiplicativity (§90), the table of σ for each prime-signature class (§88) and the recursion σ(p^n) = 1 + p·σ(p^{n-1}) (§89).

§93. For N = p^3, σ(p^3) = 1+p+p^2+p^3 = (1+p)(1+p^2), so it is always composite. If p is odd, both factors are even, so 4 | σ(p^3). Hence σ(p^3) = (1+p^2)·σ(p).

§94. For N = p^4, σ(p^4) = 1+p+p^2+p^3+p^4. This is always odd: for odd p it is a sum of five odd terms, and for p = 2 it is 1 plus even terms. It can therefore be prime, e.g. σ(2^4) = 31.

§95. For N = p^5, σ(p^5) = (1+p+p^2)(1+p^3), and 1+p^3 = (1+p)(1-p+p^2). So σ(p^5) = (1+p)(1+p+p^2)(1-p+p^2) = (1-p+p^2)·σ(p)·σ(p^2), which is composite.

§96. If gcd(M,N) = 1, then σ(MN) = σ(M)σ(N). So σ(N) has more factors the more distinct primes enter N.

§97. Claim: for any N and prime p, σ(Np) > p·σ(N). Reason: the divisors of Np include every p·d with d | N, which sum to p·σ(N). They also include divisors of N not divisible by p (at least d = 1), which are not of that form.

§98 (case p ∤ N). By multiplicativity, σ(Np) = (1+p)σ(N) = pσ(N) + σ(N) > pσ(N).

§99 (case p | N). Write N = M·p^n; Euler leaves p ∤ M implicit [my addition]. Then σ(N) = σ(M)σ(p^n) and σ(Np) = σ(M)σ(p^{n+1}). Using §89, σ(p^{n+1}) = 1 + pσ(p^n). So σ(Np) = σ(M) + p·σ(p^n)σ(M) = pσ(N) + σ(M) > pσ(N).

§100. A table of σ(n) for n = 1,…,60.

§101 announces the list of integers ≤ 60 that are not values of σ. The list itself is on the next page.

Purpose: §97–99 is the lemma σ(an) > aσ(n) for a > 1. The next page uses it in §104 to analyse the equation σ(N)/N = m/n. That analysis leads in §106–108 to the Euclid–Euler characterization of even perfect numbers and the odd perfect number question.
errors: No mathematical errors found. All 60 table entries are correct.
§99 tacitly assumes p ∤ M; this is needed for σ(Mp^n) = σ(M)σ(p^n) and is implied by the case split with §98.
§93: 'ad minimum divisibilis per 4' is correct for odd p. Sharper: 1+p^2 ≡ 2 (mod 4), so 8 | σ(p^3) exactly when p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Not an error, just not stated.
§97's verbal argument is valid; strictness comes from the divisor 1 (and any other divisor not divisible by p).

results.what: σ(p^3) = (1+p)(1+p^2), divisible by 4 for odd prime p

results.what: σ(Np) > pσ(N) for prime p, more precisely σ(Np) = pσ(N) + σ(M) with N = Mp^n, p ∤ M
results.modern_name: inequality σ(an) > aσ(n) (a > 1); abundancy index σ(n)/n increases under taking multiples
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (used in his proof of the even perfect number theorem)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792), published posthumously in 1849. The material is elementary divisor-sum theory that Euler also published in his lifetime (e.g. the papers on σ and on amicable/perfect numbers). Nothing here is unknown or attributed to later authors.

checkable.asserts: σ(p^3) divisible by 4 for odd primes

checkable.sympy: all(divisor_sigma(q**4) % 2 == 1 for q in primerange(2, 1000)) and divisor_sigma(16) == 31
expand(sum(p**k for k in range(6)) - (1+p+p**2)*(1+p**3)) == 0 and expand((1+p**3) - (1+p)*(1-p+p**2)) == 0
all(divisor_sigma(N*q) > q*divisor_sigma(N) for N in range(1, 300) for q in primerange(2, 50))
all(divisor_sigma(M*q**(n+1)) == q*divisor_sigma(M*q**n) + divisor_sigma(M) for M in range(1, 60) for q in primerange(2, 20) for n in range(0, 4) if M % q != 0)
checkable.asserts: σ(Np) = pσ(N) + σ(M) for N = Mp^n, p ∤ M (§99)
the list of non-values of σ up to 60 announced in §101 (given on the next page) is correct

§99: the image reads '∫Np = ∫M ∫p^{n+1}' (product), consistent with the transcription.
